description:
Aspirational benchmark ideas that are not yet ready for implementation. When an idea is ready, create a dedicated tracker item with full tasks, decision gates, guardrails, and acceptance criteria, then mark it here as promoted.

Re-triaged 2026-09-25. Each entry below records its status and dated evidence. The legacy work units (w1-w12) in this item's `legacy` section predate this triage. Use the status map here, not the legacy `pending` flags.

## Status map for the legacy work units
- w1-w4 (graph benchmark: Neo4j/Neptune, LDBC SNB, query-language strategy, workload): **split**. The SQL-expressible part is ready to promote (see 'Promote now'). Native graph engines stay here.
- w5-w8 (interactive benchmark explorer web UI): **superseded, done elsewhere**. BenchBox ships the Results Explorer (`results-explorer/`: Preact + Vite + DuckDB-WASM, static, no server API), which answers w6 (users/use cases), w7 (tech stack: no Flask/FastAPI backend), and w8 (results API: static snapshots queried in-browser). Explorer follow-ups are tracked in their own items (e.g. rework-results-secondary-navigation-information-architecture). Nothing remains here.
- w9-w12 (streaming: Kafka/Flink/Spark Streaming, Nexmark, TSBS overlap, broker vs processor): **stays in backlog**, with updated findings below.
- Geospatial: was already removed from this backlog. It is tracked as the tracker item `geospatial-primitives-benchmark`. The old path `TODO/benchmark-expansion/planning/geospatial-primitives-benchmark.yaml` no longer exists: `_project/TODO` holds only `_indexes`.

## Promote now: SQL graph analytics based on LDBC SNB BI
- LDBC's official BI repository (github.com/ldbc/ldbc_snb_bi, Apache-2.0, last pushed 2026-04-07) contains an Umbra implementation of all 20 BI queries written in PostgreSQL-dialect SQL (`umbra/queries/bi-1..20.sql`). Path queries (Q15, Q19, Q20) use `WITH RECURSIVE` bidirectional BFS, and parameters use psql `\set`, which BenchBox would substitute. No graph engine is required.
- Pre-generated datasets are on Cloudflare R2 (datasets.ldbcouncil.org/bi-pre-audit/, composite-merged-fk and projected-fk CSV formats) at SF1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000, and 10000, with md5 checksums. Substitution parameters cover SF1-SF30000. SF10 validation outputs generated by Umbra exist for answer checking. No Spark datagen is needed.
- Fit: runs on BenchBox's existing SQL platforms, notably DuckDB, PostgreSQL, and CedarDB (Umbra's successor), and stresses recursive CTEs, deep joins, and many-to-many traversal, which TPC workloads don't cover.
- Constraints to carry into the promoted item:
  (a) Only audited results may be called 'LDBC Benchmark Results', so name it as 'derived from LDBC SNB BI'.
  (b) The dataset licence is unverified; confirm before shipping a downloader (precedent: seek-formal-legal-review-of-imdb-dataverse-terms).
  (c) Recursive-CTE support varies by platform, so gate per platform.
  (d) Validate against the published SF10 Umbra outputs, and DuckDB at SF1.

## Backlog, step 1 (prerequisite for step 2): full-text search on log data (TextBench)
Source: github.com/ClickHouse/TextBench (Apache-2.0, last pushed 2026-04-23), read 2026-09-25.

What it is:
- A full-text search benchmark over log data, published by ClickHouse, comparing ClickHouse and Elasticsearch.
- Dataset: synthetic OpenTelemetry logs from the OpenTelemetry demo application. 50B rows covering one day (2025-09-23), as Parquet with 1B rows per file sorted by Timestamp: `part_000`-`part_049` in the public bucket `s3://public-pme/text_bench/` (eu-west-3; HTTPS base `https://public-pme.s3.eu-west-3.amazonaws.com/text_bench`). Schema: Timestamp, TraceId, SpanId, TraceFlags, SeverityText, SeverityNumber, ServiceName, Body (the full-text field), and ResourceAttributes / ScopeAttributes / LogAttributes (string maps). Official scales: 1B (part_000), 10B (part_000-009), 50B (all).
- Queries: 9 (the README's heading says Q1-Q10, but it lists Q1-Q9). The set is deliberately limited to features both engines support: single-token, AND, and OR token matching, combined with service, severity, and time-range predicates, producing count(), GROUP BY service, hourly histograms, and time-ordered fetch with LIMIT 100. Phrase matching and wildcards are explicitly excluded.
- Method: ingest, restart, three runs per query (cold = run 1 after restart; hot = best of runs 2-3). Records data size plus text-index size. AWS m6i.8xlarge (32 vCPU, 128 GiB), gp3 16K IOPS, single node.

Why this goes first:
(a) It owns the dataset and schema that SearchBench reuses. SearchBench's `lib/download-otel-logs` reads the same `text_bench` bucket, and SearchBench's Q01-Q83 are derived from TextBench. Building TextBench first delivers the shared foundation: dataset downloader and slicer, otel_logs DDL per platform, map-column handling, index-build phase reporting, and the per-platform query-variant mechanism.
(b) Every query has an exact answer: counts, aggregations, and rows ordered by timestamp, with no relevance scores. It can use BenchBox's existing exact-match validation against DuckDB. It avoids SearchBench's hardest open problem (ranking equivalence).
(c) It is small (9 queries) and the most portable subset: token matching is expressible on DuckDB (fts or plain tokenized predicates), PostgreSQL (GIN FTS), ClickHouse (hasToken, hasAllTokens, hasAnyTokens), SereneDB, Doris/StarRocks/Databend inverted indexes, and Snowflake/BigQuery SEARCH().

Design notes for when it is promoted:
- Queries are ClickHouse SQL (and Elasticsearch DSL). BenchBox needs per-platform query variants registered in sql_compat (precedent: query_source/vector_search_variants.py), plus a capability matrix. Token semantics differ (tokenizer, case folding, punctuation), so each variant must document its tokenization and be validated to produce the same match counts as the reference.
- There is no official scale below 1B rows. BenchBox needs its own smaller scales (e.g. 1M, 10M, 100M) sliced from part_000.parquet with HTTP byte-range reads, as SearchBench's `lib/slice_parquet.py` does. The data is time-sorted, so slices cover shorter time ranges; the time-bounded queries (Q1, Q6: a 30-minute window at 00:00) still hit data, but the 1-hour histograms get fewer buckets. Record this per scale.
- Report load time, index-build time, data size, and index size separately.
- ClickHouse authored it, so BenchBox owns its own per-platform tuning and must not treat ClickHouse's configuration as a neutral default.
- Confirm the dataset licence or terms before shipping a downloader. The repository is Apache-2.0, but the bucket contents' terms were not checked.

Suggested first slice: 100M-row slice; DuckDB, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse (local or server), and SereneDB once its adapter lands; all 9 queries; exact validation against DuckDB.

## Backlog, step 2 (depends on step 1): search plus analytics on log data (SearchBench)
Sources: SereneDB blog 'SearchBench vs ClickHouse' (https://serenedb.com/blog/searchbench-clickhouse) and github.com/serenedb/searchbench (Apache-2.0, last pushed 2026-09-25), read 2026-09-25.

What it adds on top of TextBench:
- The same TextBench dataset and bucket, with smoke scales of 100k, 1m, and 100m rows sliced by byte-range reads, and 1B, 10B, and 50B full scales. SereneDB reports 11.2 GiB on disk at 100M rows and 112.2 GiB at 1B.
- 92 queries. Q01-Q83 are derived from and expand on TextBench: frequency-tagged variants of boolean token match (term, AND, OR, negation, min-match), plus phrase and proximity; prefix, suffix, wildcard, regexp, and fuzzy matching; BM25-ranked top-K; time-ordered log tailing; and GROUP BY aggregations. Q84-Q92 are joins on TraceId.
- Engines in the repo: SereneDB, ClickHouse (sorted and unsorted), Elasticsearch (incl. columnar), OpenSearch, ParadeDB, vanilla Postgres FTS, TigerData (incl. columnstore), CrateDB, ArangoDB, Manticore, Quickwit, VictoriaLogs.
- Method: ClickBench-style runner (install/start/stop/check/load/query/data-size scripts per engine). GCP n2-standard-32. Three runs per query, best of the last two reported. Page cache dropped for cold runs. 60 s timeout. Single client, single node.
- Headline claim (10B rows, hot): SereneDB 173.5 ms median with 92/92 finished; ClickHouse sorted 1912.5 ms with 60/92; unsorted 2301.0 ms with 48/92. ClickHouse's text index has no BM25, so 22 queries are unsupported. Treat these as vendor-reported and unverified.

Additional blockers beyond step 1:
(a) Ranking equivalence. BM25 scores and top-K membership depend on analyzer settings, so exact-match validation fails for ranked queries. It needs a documented contract: exact for boolean-match counts and aggregations; overlap/recall tolerance for ranked top-K. SearchBench ships `lib/check_results.py`, which is worth studying.
(b) Pattern queries (regexp, wildcard, fuzzy) run as scans on engines without a suitable index. Register them as capability-gated rather than letting them time out.
(c) Vendor authorship. SereneDB wrote the benchmark and its adapters, so BenchBox must own its own query variants and tuning.
(d) Engines without SQL (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Quickwit, VictoriaLogs) are out of scope unless reached through an SQL interface.
(e) Scale: 1B+ rows needs over 100 GiB. Local work is limited to the smoke scales; larger scales are live-cloud or native-Linux runs and need approval.

Related: serenedb-search-benchmarks (SereneDB-specific search enablement) should share the step 1/step 2 query-variant design.

Re-evaluate when: step 1 lands, or a user asks for text-search comparisons across BenchBox platforms. Step 1's own trigger: the SereneDB adapter lands (serenedb-adapter-core), or any request for full-text search coverage.

## Stays in backlog: native graph engines and graph query languages
- GQL (ISO/IEC 39075) was published 2024-04-11. Neo4j Cypher now covers most mandatory GQL features. Neptune (openCypher/Gremlin/SPARQL) is cloud-only.
- Kùzu (embedded graph DB, a natural local candidate) was archived on 2025-10-10 after Apple acquired Kùzu Inc. Community forks exist (LadybugDB, Bighorn). Wait until a fork proves durable.
- SQL/PGQ (SQL:2023 part 16): PostgreSQL 19 committed it (2026-03-16) but reverted it on 2026-09-07. The earliest it could return is PostgreSQL 20 (about September 2027). DuckPGQ (DuckDB community extension) works but has reported compatibility limits with newer DuckDB patch releases. Oracle 23ai supports SQL/PGQ, but Oracle has no BenchBox adapter (see platform-expansion-evaluation-2026-09).
- Re-evaluate when: PostgreSQL 20 ships SQL/PGQ, DuckPGQ tracks DuckDB releases reliably, or a Kùzu fork reaches a stable release. The natural next step then is a SQL/PGQ variant of the promoted LDBC-derived workload, not a separate Cypher/Gremlin adapter family.

## Stays in backlog: streaming benchmarks (Nexmark)
- Nexmark is the de facto streaming-SQL benchmark (a 27-query set as run by RisingWave against Flink). Relevant engines: Apache Flink SQL, RisingWave and Materialize (both PostgreSQL-wire, and sqlglot ships dialects for both), and Spark Structured Streaming.
- Blocker: BenchBox measures bounded batch query timings. Streaming needs a sustained event source, continuous queries or materialized views, and throughput/latency metrics. That is a new measurement subsystem, not a benchmark add-on.
- w11 resolved: TSBS DevOps (`benchbox/tsbs_devops.py`) is batch time-series querying and does not overlap with continuous stream processing.
- w12 resolved: benchmark the processing engines (Flink, RisingWave, Materialize). Kafka is only the source and should not be benchmarked as an engine.
- Re-evaluate when there is sponsorship or user demand. A cheaper first step, if wanted: run Nexmark's queries as batch SQL over generated bounded event tables on existing platforms (no streaming semantics), clearly labeled as such.
